sections.b: The book opens with a preface (Proverbs 1:1–7) that names its aim, "knowing wisdom and discipline", and its foundation: "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7). Then come about ten talks of a father to his son, broken by speeches of Wisdom as a woman (Proverbs 1:20–33; 8; 9:1–6). The talks warn against violent companions and the strange woman and urge the son to seek wisdom like silver. The introduction ends with two feasts, Wisdom's and Folly's, who call the same naive passers-by with the same words (Proverbs 9:4, 16). Most scholars think chapters 1–9 were written last, as the gateway to the older collections, so that the short sayings of chapters 10–29 would be read by someone who has already chosen Wisdom's road.

In Proverbs 1–9 wisdom becomes a woman who speaks. She shouts in the streets and warns those who ignore her (Proverbs 1:20–33), stands at the city gates offering words better than gold (Proverbs 8:1–21), and builds a house of seven pillars where she spreads bread and wine for the naive (Proverbs 9:1–6). In Proverbs 8:22–31 she tells her origin: "The LORD acquired me, the first of his way" (Proverbs 8:22); she was born before the deeps and the mountains and was beside God as a craftsman, his delight, as he made the world.

Readers have taken her as a poetic personification of God's wisdom (most critical scholars), as the Torah, created before the world as its plan (Sirach 24; Genesis Rabbah 1:1), or as the eternal Son and Word of God (the church fathers, following John 1 and Colossians 1). Some trace her imagery to the Egyptian Maat. Her opposite is Woman Folly (Proverbs 9:13–18), who echoes the strange woman of Proverbs 2, 5 and 7.
sections.refs: Proverbs 1:20–33; Proverbs 3:13–20; Proverbs 8:1–36; Proverbs 9:1–18; Sirach 24:1–23; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–8:1; John 1:1–3; 1 Corinthians 1:24

sections.h: The fear of the LORD as the beginning
sections.b: Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10 frame the introduction with the motto that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge and of wisdom; Job 28:28 and Psalm 111:10 say the same. 'Beginning' (reshit, techillah) may mean first step, chief part or foundation. Proverbs defines the fear of the LORD as hating evil (Proverbs 8:13). The claim sets Israel's wisdom apart from its neighbors': skill in living begins with reverence for the God of Israel.
sections.refs: Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10; Proverbs 8:13; Proverbs 15:33; Job 28:28; Psalm 111:10

common: Lady Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is a picture of Christ, the Wisdom of God.
uncommon: Lady Wisdom preserves the memory of a Hebrew goddess of wisdom (Bernhard Lang).

sections.b: Early Christians read Wisdom's words in Proverbs 8 as the Son speaking. The Greek of Proverbs 8:22 reads 'The Lord created me', and about AD 318 Arius argued from it that the Son was the first creature, so that 'there was when he was not'. The Council of Nicaea (325) answered that the Son is 'begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father'. Athanasius explained 'created' as the human nature the Word took for the work of salvation, and 'he begets me' (Proverbs 8:25) as his eternal birth. Jehovah's Witnesses today read the passage as Arius did, rendering 'Jehovah produced me'.

John's prologue says that the Word was with God in the beginning and that all things came into being through him (John 1:1–3). Many scholars hear in this the language of Wisdom in Proverbs 8:22–31, who was with the LORD before creation and beside him as he made the world, and of Wisdom of Solomon 7–9 and Sirach 24, where Wisdom comes from God's mouth and dwells among people. Philo of Alexandria joined Wisdom and the Logos in the same period. The early church read Proverbs 8 as the Word speaking, which made the verse central in the fourth-century debates.
sections.refs: Proverbs 8:22–31; John 1:1–14; Sirach 24:3–8; Wisdom of Solomon 9:1–2

sections.b: Sirach identifies Wisdom with 'the law that Moses commanded us' (Sirach 24:23), and Baruch 4:1 calls her 'the book of the commandments of God'. The rabbis read Proverbs 8 accordingly. Genesis Rabbah 1:1 makes the Torah the 'craftsman's tool' (Proverbs 8:30) that God consulted like an architect's plan when he created the world, and reads Genesis 1:1 'with reshit', because the Torah is called reshit in Proverbs 8:22. The Mishnah names the Torah first among the things God 'acquired' (Mishnah Avot 6:10) and calls it the 'precious instrument by which the world was created' (Avot 3:14, quoting Proverbs 4:2). Proverbs 3:17–18, 'a tree of life to those who grab hold of her', is sung of the Torah in the synagogue.
sections.refs: Proverbs 3:17–18; Proverbs 4:2; Proverbs 6:20–23; Proverbs 8:22–31; Sirach 24:23; Baruch 4:1

sections.b: Proverbs says that "It was by wisdom that the LORD founded the earth" (Proverbs 3:19), and in Proverbs 8:22–31 Wisdom describes the making of the world from her own point of view: the deeps and springs, the mountains, the heavens, the circle drawn on the face of the deep, the limit set for the sea. There is no battle with the sea, as in some psalms; the sea simply obeys. The point is that the world has an order that wisdom can learn, and that a life lived by wisdom fits the grain of creation.

sections.h: Drink from your own well: Proverbs 5
sections.b: Proverbs 5 warns a young man against the strange woman and then praises married love in images of water: drink from your own cistern, let your spring be blessed, "Take your joy from the woman you married when you were young" (Proverbs 5:18), be lost in love for her always. The frankness matches the Song of Songs, and the phrase 'the wife of your youth' returns in Malachi 2:14. Proverbs 6:20–35 and 7 add the costs of adultery: a jealous husband who will accept no ransom, and a road to Sheol.
sections.refs: Proverbs 2:16–19; Proverbs 5:15–20; Proverbs 6:24–35; Proverbs 7:1–27; Malachi 2:14–16; Song of Songs 4:12–15

sections.b: Proverbs calls the seductress of chapters 2, 5, 6 and 7 the zarah, 'strange woman', and the nokhriyyah, 'foreign woman'. Most interpreters think she is an Israelite adulteress, 'strange' because she belongs to another man (Proverbs 2:17; 7:19). Others, such as Joseph Blenkinsopp and Harold Washington, link the language with Judea after the exile, when marriages to women outside the community were a burning question (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27), and read the warnings partly as warnings against such marriages.
sections.refs: Proverbs 2:16–17; Proverbs 5:20; Proverbs 6:24; Proverbs 7:5; Ezra 10:2; Nehemiah 13:23–27; 1 Kings 11:1–8

sections.h: Wisdom as a tree of life
sections.b: The phrase from Eden returns four times in Proverbs, always for something within reach: wisdom (Proverbs 3:18), the fruit of the righteous (11:30), a longing fulfilled (13:12) and a gentle tongue (15:4). In Proverbs 3:18 Wisdom is a tree of life "To those who grab hold of her": what was barred to Adam and Eve is offered again through wisdom. Jewish liturgy sings the verse of the Torah.
sections.refs: Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 11:30; Proverbs 13:12; Proverbs 15:4; Genesis 2:9; Genesis 3:22–24; Revelation 22:2

sections.b: Proverbs 1–9 is full of road words: way, path, track, lane. Proverbs 4:10–19 sets out the two roads in their clearest form: the road of the righteous "is like the first gleam of morning, which keeps getting brighter until the day stands at noon" (Proverbs 4:18), while the wicked walk in darkness and do not know what makes them stumble. The introduction ends with two houses on the same heights, Wisdom's leading to life and Folly's to Sheol (Proverbs 9).

Proverbs 6:16–19 lists "six things" the LORD hates, "and seven" that are abhorrent to him: proud eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that plans trouble, feet that run to evil, a false witness, and one who sets brothers quarreling. The list runs down the body and ends with the climax, the one who destroys community.

Proverbs 6:1–5 tells a son who has stood good for his neighbor (struck palms on the pledge) to get free at once: humble himself, badger the man, and not sleep until he is out, like a gazelle escaping a hunter. Standing surety could cost a man his property or his freedom. The warning returns in Proverbs 11:15, 17:18, 20:16, 22:26–27 and 27:13.
sections.refs: Proverbs 6:1–5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 22:26–27; Genesis 43:9; Hebrews 7:22

sections.b: "Go to the ant, you lazy one" (Proverbs 6:6): the ant has no chief or officer, yet it stores food in summer. Proverbs 6:10–11, repeated in 24:33–34, mocks the lazy one's 'a little sleep' and warns that poverty arrives like an armed robber. The Greek adds a second example, the bee.

sections.h: Echoes of the Shema in Proverbs
sections.b: The father of Proverbs speaks of his teaching in the words of Deuteronomy 6: tie it on your heart and neck (Proverbs 6:21), on your fingers (7:3); it will guide you when you walk, guard you when you lie down and talk with you when you wake (6:22). Wisdom's disciple waits at the 'doorposts' (mezuzot) of her house (8:34). The parent's teaching is presented as continuous with the covenant.

sections.h: The strange woman's house and Sheol
sections.b: In Proverbs 1–9 the road to the strange woman's house is the road to Sheol: her house sinks to death and her tracks lead to the shades (Proverbs 2:18), her steps take hold of Sheol (5:5), her house is "Roads to Sheol" (7:27), and Folly's guests are already "down in Sheol's depths" (9:18). Sheol here is less a place of punishment than the end of life that folly brings early.

Wisdom's invitation, "Come, have some of my bread, and drink the wine I mixed" (Proverbs 9:5), was read by Cyprian (Letter 63) and Augustine (City of God 17.20) as a figure of the Eucharist, with Wisdom's house as the Church. Jewish readers took the bread as the Torah. Jesus' 'I am the bread of life' (John 6:35) uses a similar invitation.

Proverbs opens with "The proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel" (Proverbs 1:1). Jewish tradition heard Solomon recalling David's teaching in Proverbs 4:3–4, since David calls Solomon 'young and tender' in 1 Chronicles 22:5 and 29:1, with the same word for 'tender' (rakh). Most modern scholars think chapters 1–9 were written centuries later and placed under Solomon's name as Israel's model sage.
